articles.title: Front-row seats to orbit: How La Cañada Flintridge watches SpaceX from the driveway
articles.image_alt: Twilight rocket plume over the foothills, viewed from a west-facing deck
articles.image_prompt: Photorealistic twilight from a La Cañada Flintridge hillside deck looking west. A Falcon 9 twilight plume blooms as a pale glowing space jellyfish over the San Gabriels. Warm deck lights, no people, no logos, no text.
articles.excerpt: As a resident of La Cañada Flintridge, you already have something most of the country has to book a flight for: front-row access to rocket launches tied to the engineers in your own community. You do not need a badge, a viewing stand, or a trip to Florida. On the right evening, the show starts over the western horizon, climbs through twilight, and turns the sky into a glowing jellyfish while dinner is still on the table.

articles.title: The little-known origin of JPL: Caltech’s Suicide Squad got kicked into a wash and founded the space age
articles.image_alt: Early rocket motor experiment in the Arroyo Seco, 1936
articles.excerpt: Here is the part the Mars rover press releases never lead with. NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory did not begin as a gleaming federal campus on Oak Grove Drive. It began because a handful of Caltech kids — plus two amateurs who were not even enrolled — kept blowing things up on campus, and the Institute decided the safest place for that hobby was a dry riverbed.
